806.title: Block close: the first thousand years
806.hook: martyrs, monks, creeds, alphabets, and a church spread across continents
806.howItsDone: Christians remember the saints and martyrs of the early church in their calendars, names and churches; Catholic and Orthodox Christians keep their feast days, and some Protestant churches honor them as examples of faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vladimir's envoys, and your line was heaven or earth? They couldn't tell, standing in that church. Where did beauty stop you long enough to wonder? Day eight hundred six.

A stadium, packed, rows rising up into the dark. And down on the track, one runner, tired, still going. That's roughly the picture the letter to the Hebrews paints. After a long chapter naming the faithful of the past, Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab and more, it turns to the reader: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses." The stands are full. So, at the end of this block of the path, we look up at them. Today's word is witnesses.

This block began with the apostles scattering: they went everywhere. Peter and Paul in Rome. The temple falling, the gospels written down before memories faded. Then the martyrs: Ignatius on the road, calling himself God's wheat; Polycarp; Perpetua and Felicity, a noblewoman and an enslaved woman, sisters in the arena. Christians who stayed in the plague when others fled. Seed, not end. Then a turn: Constantine, a letter granting freedom for all, and the councils. Nicaea and its creed, true God from true God, and Athanasius standing against the world. Then the monks and the builders of mercy: Antony in the desert, Pachomius' community, Basil's city for the sick, Macrina the teacher of teachers, Benedict asking monks to listen with the ear of the heart. Then the long reach of it. Patrick and Brigid in Ireland, Columba on Iona, Hilda at Whitby, Caedmon finding his song in the stable, Bede finishing his work. And east and south: Ethiopia, Armenia, the Thomas Christians of Kerala, monks with books arriving in China. Ephrem's women's choirs. A dome that seemed to hang from heaven. Icons broken and carried home again. An oak felled, an alphabet made, envoys who couldn't tell heaven from earth. It's a lot. And it isn't tidy. There were quarrels, splits, emperors who used the church and Christians who used power badly. The path has tried to say so. But Hebrews' picture holds. These aren't statues in a museum. In the letter's image, they're in the stands, and the race is still on. The verse goes on, in the King James words: "let us run with patience the race that is set before us." Tomorrow a new block begins, the middle centuries, east and west, starting with a monastery where the prayer hardly stopped.
screen: then, large: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one person from this block to remember. Settle, and breathe. Let the names drift past: Perpetua, Antony, Macrina, Patrick, Bede, Ephrem, Thomas, Boniface, the envoys, or one I haven't named. Don't pick the most important. Pick the one who stuck. Ask yourself why that one. Is it their courage, their kindness, their stubbornness, their song? Hold that person in mind as if they were sitting in the stands, watching your race. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. If you don't, just thank them, quietly, across the centuries. The bell holds the time.
Witnesses. The cloud of the faithful dead the letter to the Hebrews pictures filling the stands: apostles, martyrs, monks, creeds, alphabets, a church spread across continents.
Your line: a great cloud. Today, tell someone about the person you named, in two sentences, so their story gets one more listener. Day eight hundred six.

807.title: Cluny
807.hook: a reforming monastery whose monks prayed almost without stopping
807.howItsDone: Monks and nuns in Benedictine communities still gather at set hours of the day and night to sing the psalms, and some Christians outside monasteries pray shorter forms of those hours in the morning and evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the block on the church's first long stretch, a great cloud of witnesses, and your line was a great cloud. Whose name did you choose to remember from it? A new block starts today. Day eight hundred seven.

A duke sits down to give away a piece of his own land. His name is William, and the land is a place called Cluny, in Burgundy. In the charter he signs, he doesn't hand it to a bishop or a king. He gives it to the apostles Peter and Paul, for a house of monks. Then he adds something unusual. Nobody, not his own heirs, not a prince, not even a bishop, is to interfere with them. The monks will choose their own abbot. Why would a powerful man tie his own hands like that? Because he wanted one thing done there, without interruption, for good. Today's word is the place where it was done.

The thing done at Cluny was prayer. The charter places Cluny's monks under the Rule of Saint Benedict, which sets prayer at fixed hours through the day and the night, and says nothing is to be put before the work of God. The Rule leans on a line from the Psalms, in the King James words: "Seven times a day do I praise thee." Cluny took that and kept going. Its monks are remembered for adding psalms, processions and long prayers for the dead, until the singing in the church seemed hardly to stop. Behind it all sits a short line from Paul's first letter to the church at Thessalonica, in the King James wording: "Pray without ceasing." Christians have read that line in more than one way. Some, like the Cluny monks, read it as a schedule: build a life where the prayer never stops, because someone is always at it. Some Orthodox Christians read it as a prayer carried inward, a short line repeated until it travels along with the breath. Some Protestants hear it as a posture: a whole day turned toward God, at the sink and on the bus. The readings don't cancel each other. And Cluny's way spread. Tradition remembers other monasteries asking to be reformed by it and joining its family of houses. Later critics, as this path will see, thought it grew too rich. But at its heart was a simple, stubborn idea: that somewhere, someone should always be praying.

Here's the practice: stay a little longer than you planned. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, pray the way you usually do, and when you reach the place where you normally stop, don't stop. Stay a little more. You might repeat a line you already know, or simply keep company in silence. If you don't pray, sit with your breath, and when the urge to get up arrives, notice it, and stay anyway. At Cluny, one psalm led into the next. Let the bell decide when you stop. The bell holds the time.
Cluny. A monastery in Burgundy, given to the apostles and left free, where the monks' prayer seemed never to stop.

Your line: prayer without ceasing. Today, pick one ordinary thing you do over and over, rinsing a cup, opening a door, and let it be a small turn toward God, or toward stillness, each time it comes around. Day eight hundred seven.

808.title: 1054, told slowly
808.hook: a papal envoy lays a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia, and the break hardens
808.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox churches both pray for Christian unity in their services, and their leaders have met and issued joint statements, while still differing on questions such as the authority of the pope.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cluny, and your line was prayer without ceasing. Which ordinary thing became a small turn toward God, or toward stillness? Day eight hundred eight.

Constantinople, the great church of Hagia Sophia, and the liturgy is about to begin. Envoys from Rome walk up toward the altar. Their leader is Cardinal Humbert. He lays a document on the altar: a bull of excommunication against the city's patriarch, Michael Cerularius. Then the envoys turn and walk out, shaking the dust from their feet. By one account, one of the clergy runs after them and begs them to take it back. They refuse, and the document ends up on the floor. Soon after, the patriarch and his synod answer with an excommunication of their own. Today's word is the year in the title. And we're going to tell it slowly.

Told slowly, it's less a single slam than a long drift. East and West had been growing apart: Greek and Latin, different customs at the altar, a dispute over wording in the creed, and the question of how far the authority of the bishop of Rome reaches. Then that day in the great church. Notice what was excommunicated. Not whole churches. The documents named people. The bull named the patriarch and those with him; the patriarch's synod answered against the envoys. The break hardened afterward, through later wounds this path will come to. Scripture has a word for a split like this. In Mark, Jesus says no one sews new cloth onto an old garment, or, in the King James words, "the rent is made worse." In Mark's Greek, that rent is a schisma, a tear in cloth. The church borrowed the word for its own tears. And the hope runs back to Jesus's prayer in John, in the King James words: "That they all may be one." Much later, a pope, Paul the sixth, and a patriarch of Constantinople, Athenagoras, issued a joint statement. They regretted those old excommunications and wished to remove them from the memory of the church. Later still, Pope John Paul the second used a picture for East and West that became today's line: the church should breathe with both its lungs. Catholics and Orthodox Christians still differ on real questions, and each church describes the division in its own terms. The Orthodox liturgy prays for the union of all. Catholics pray for unity too. Both lungs, still learning to breathe together.
screen: `A LONG DRIFT, NOT A SINGLE SLAM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: settle, and breathe all the way in. Feel both sides of your chest rise. Then breathe out. Do it again, slowly. If you pray, you can pray Jesus's own line, that they all may be one, holding Catholic and Orthodox Christians together in mind: a parish you know, an icon you've seen, a name. If you don't pray, simply keep breathing, and notice two lungs working together without arguing over which one leads. Let each breath hold both. The bell holds the time.
Schisma. The Greek word for a tear in cloth, borrowed for the slow-hardening split of ten fifty-four between East and West, with excommunications traded between envoys and a patriarch.

Your line: both lungs. Today, take one deep breath on purpose, deep enough to feel both sides fill, and let it remind you of one quarrel that could still heal, in the church or closer to home. Day eight hundred eight.

809.title: Faith seeking understanding
809.hook: Anselm of Canterbury: I believe so that I may understand
809.howItsDone: Christians often bring questions about faith to study groups, classes, books and conversations with pastors or priests, and Anselm's phrase is still used to describe theology as faith that asks questions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the long, slow schisma between East and West, and your line was both lungs. Which quarrel came to mind when you took that deep breath? Day eight hundred nine.

A monk in Normandy can't put a question down. He's Anselm, prior of the abbey of Bec, and one day he'll be archbishop of Canterbury. He had already written one book about God at his brothers' request. Now he wanted something that sounds simple: a single short argument. He searched, and by his own account he nearly gave up. He tried to push the idea away like a distraction. It wouldn't leave. His biographer says it troubled his sleep and his meals, and even his prayers. Then, one night, it came clear. He wrote it down, not as a lecture, but as a prayer, spoken to God. And he gave it a first title that became a motto. Today's word is that title.
screen: `A MONK WHO CAN'T PUT A QUESTION DOWN.`

segments.voice: Anselm called the book the Proslogion, an address. In its preface he says his first title for it was faith seeking understanding. And its first chapter ends with words people still quote. In paraphrase: I don't try to understand so that I can believe. I believe so that I can understand. In Latin, credo ut intelligam. Hear what that does and doesn't say. It doesn't say: switch off your mind and believe. And it doesn't say: believe nothing until it's proven. It says faith comes first, and then faith goes looking. It asks. It argues. It wants to know what it loves. Watch how the book begins. Before any argument, Anselm invites himself to step away from his busy thoughts for a little while and seek God's face. Then he reasons, out loud, in front of God. The New Testament has its own version. The first letter of Peter, in the King James words, asks believers to "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you." A reason for the hope. Not a slogan. Then a monk named Gaunilo read Anselm's argument and wrote a reply, pushing back hard. Anselm answered him, and asked that the critic's reply and his own response travel together with the book. Questions welcomed, answers shown in public. Christians have used the motto in different ways. Some theologians build whole systems on it. For other readers it's simpler: belief and questions can sit at the same table.
screen: `I BELIEVE SO THAT I MAY UNDERSTAND.`
`THE CRITIC'S REPLY GOES IN THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask one honest question. Settle, and breathe. Let a question rise that you don't usually say out loud. About God. About something you were taught. About why you're on this path at all. Don't answer it yet. Just let it be asked, plainly, in your own words. If you pray, you can ask it in prayer, the way Anselm spoke his straight to God. If you don't, hold it like an object in your hands and turn it over slowly. Questions are welcome here. The bell holds the time.
Proslogion. Anselm's book, whose first title was faith seeking understanding: belief that keeps asking, so that it can understand.
Your line: faith seeks understanding. Today, write your question down somewhere you'll find it again, and look for one good thing to read about it, or one person to ask. Day eight hundred nine.

810.title: The crusades, honestly
810.hook: armed pilgrimages that killed Muslims, Jews and Eastern Christians; crusaders sacked Constantinople; later popes apologized
810.howItsDone: Churches remember the crusades in different ways; the Catholic Church has asked forgiveness for violence done by its members, and some Christians take part in services of repentance and in work for reconciliation with Jews, Muslims and Orthodox Christians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anselm and his Proslogion, and your line was faith seeks understanding. What question did you write down, and where did you go looking? Day eight hundred ten.

"God wills it." One chronicler says that is what a crowd shouted back at a pope in an open field at Clermont, in France. The pope was Urban. The versions of his speech that reached us were written down afterward, and they don't agree word for word. But between them they carry the call: Christians in the East need help, and, in most versions, Jerusalem is the goal. Men sewed crosses onto their clothes and set out. Others followed in later expeditions. That is the beginning of what we now call the crusades. Today's word is that one, and today we tell it honestly.

Honestly means holding more than one thing. Some who went believed they were doing penance, leaving home to walk toward the city where Jesus died. And the armies did terrible things. On the way east, crusading bands attacked Jewish communities in the Rhineland; Jewish chroniclers wrote down the names and the grief. When Jerusalem fell, crusader writers themselves described the killing of the city's Muslims, and wrote of it as triumph; other sources tell of its Jews killed too. And in a later crusade, armies that had set out for the East turned on Constantinople, a Christian city, and sacked it, churches and all. A Byzantine historian who lived through it, Niketas Choniates, wrote that these men who carried the cross on their shoulders showed less mercy than the Saracens, the name then used for Muslims. The pope of the day, Innocent the third, wrote angrily against what was done. Set all that beside the Gospel. When one of his followers drew a sword in the garden, Jesus told him, in Matthew's King James words: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." Much later, the churches looked back. At a Day of Pardon, Pope John Paul the second asked forgiveness for violence some Christians had used in the service of truth. And speaking in Athens, he said the sack of Constantinople fills Catholics with deep regret. Historians still argue over motives, and different churches tell the story with different weight. Today's line comes out of that looking back: never again in his name.

Here's the practice: settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind people harmed by violence done in God's name. Jewish families in the Rhineland. The Muslims and Jews of Jerusalem. Christians in Constantinople. And people in our own time, of any faith or none. Don't rush past them; take them one group at a time. If you pray, you can pray for them, and for those who carry the memory. If you don't, hold them in silence. Then, gently, ask where faith has ever been used as a weapon in your own life, even with words. The bell holds the time.
Crusade. The armed pilgrimages called by popes and marked with a cross on the clothes, remembered now with honesty and with sorrow.
Your line: never again in his name. Today, notice when anyone, you included, reaches for God to win an argument, and choose not to. Day eight hundred ten.

811.title: Bernard and the Cistercians
811.hook: plain white habits, plain churches, farming and prayer
811.howItsDone: Cistercian monks and nuns, including the stricter Trappists, still keep the Rule of Saint Benedict in plain churches, supporting themselves by work such as farming, baking and brewing between the hours of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crusades, told honestly, and your line was never again in his name. Did you catch anyone reaching for God to win an argument? Day eight hundred eleven.

How does a hard way of life survive when almost nobody wants to join it? A new monastery in a remote place called Cîteaux, in Burgundy, is struggling. Its monks want to keep the Rule of Saint Benedict to the letter: their own manual work, plain food, plain clothes, long prayer. It's a hard life, and the early account says few came to join them. Then a young nobleman knocks at the gate, and he hasn't come alone. He's brought brothers, relatives and friends, a whole company, all asking to become monks. His name is Bernard. Before long he's sent out to found a new house in a valley called Clairvaux. Today's word is that man, and the monks who lived his way.

The Cistercians, named for Cîteaux, wanted to strip things back. Their habits were plain undyed wool, pale enough that people called them the white monks. Their churches kept to bare walls and plain glass. They farmed their own land, often in out-of-the-way valleys, and prayed the hours between the work. Bernard put the reason into sharp words. In an essay to a friend, known as his Apology, he looked at the grand churches of other monasteries, with soaring heights, costly decoration and carved monsters on the cloister columns, and asked what it was all for. In paraphrase: the church's walls shine, and its poor go without. It dresses its stones in gold and leaves its children naked. He wasn't against beauty. He wrote tender sermons on the Song of Songs, full of longing for God. He was against distraction, and against spending on stone what the hungry needed. Plainness, for the Cistercians, was its own kind of beauty: light through plain glass, stone and proportion with nothing to hide behind. Some readers hear an echo of a Gospel picture in it. Jesus, in the King James words: "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin." Nothing added, nothing missing. And, as yesterday, honesty. Bernard also preached a crusade. He also wrote that the Jews must not be attacked, and he stood against a monk who was stirring up violence against them. Catholics honor him as a saint.
screen: `WALLS SHINE, AND THE POOR GO WITHOUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one small space near you. A desk, a shelf, a windowsill, the screen in your hand. Settle and breathe first. Then look at it the way a Cistercian might look at a church: what here is helping, and what's only shouting for attention? Take one or two things away, gently, or close what you don't need. Then sit and look at the plainer space for a while. Notice what's easier to see now. If you pray, you can let the cleared space become a place for prayer. The bell holds the time.
Cistercians. The white monks of Cîteaux and Clairvaux, led by the abbot Bernard, who argued that plainness leaves room for God, and bread for the poor.
Your line: plainness is beautiful. Today, before you buy or add something, ask whether a plainer choice would do. If it would, take it, and notice what you get back. Day eight hundred eleven.

812.title: Hildegard's music
812.hook: the abbess wrote a whole cycle of chants, some still sung
812.carry: feather on the breath of god
812.howItsDone: Some monasteries and choirs still sing Hildegard's chants in worship and concerts, and Catholics honor her as a saint and a Doctor of the Church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernard and the Cistercians, the white monks, and your line was plainness is beautiful. What plainer choice did you make, and what did you get back? Day eight hundred twelve.

Nuns are singing in a stone church above the Rhine, and the melody does something strange. It leaps. It climbs high, swoops low, and hangs on a single syllable for a long, long breath before it lets go. The woman who wrote it is their abbess, Hildegard of Bingen. She wrote books of visions, letters to popes and emperors, and works on medicine and the natural world. And she wrote songs for her community to sing, gathered under the name Symphonia. Choirs still sing some of them. Today's word is that music, and the way she said it came to her.

Hildegard didn't describe her gift as cleverness. In a letter she told a story about herself. In paraphrase: a king once lifted a small feather from the ground and told it to fly. It flew, not because of anything in the feather, but because the air carried it. That, she said, was her: a feather on the breath of God. Today's line. Not a boast. A confession that she was carried. Music mattered enough to her that she fought for it. Once, church authorities placed her community under a ban, and her nuns were forbidden to sing the office aloud. Hildegard wrote to the prelates of Mainz in protest. In paraphrase: before the fall, Adam's voice joined the angels in praise. The prophets made psalms and instruments to stir hearts toward God. And those who silence singing in church without good reason should take care. Her ground was the psalms. Psalm 150, in the King James words, calls for trumpet and harp, timbrel and dance, "stringed instruments and organs," and then turns to everything that has breath, and calls it to praise. Set the feather beside the psalm, and breath is the link. The air carries the feather. Breath carries the song. Christians use music in prayer in very different ways, from silent meetings to plain hymns to full choirs, and each church has its reasons. Hildegard's way is one of them: wide, soaring, and sung.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let music carry you. If you can, play a recording of medieval chant, one of Hildegard's if you can find one, and simply listen. If you can't, sit in silence and listen to your own breath. And since this is the end of the week, let the week drift past as well: Cluny's long prayer, the slow break of ten fifty-four, Anselm's question, the crusades told honestly, Bernard's plain walls, and now this music. Let one of them stay with you. If you pray, you can let the music be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Hildegard's music. The soaring chants an abbess on the Rhine wrote for her nuns, made, as she understood it, by a feather on the breath of God.
Your line: feather on the breath of God. Today, let one piece of music do the praying for you, in the car or the kitchen, and do nothing else while it plays. Day eight hundred twelve.
